title: How plants are grouped: by the way they make new plants

summary.text: Ferns and mosses never make a flower or a seed, yet new ferns and mosses keep appearing on wet walls. They grow from spores, single cells far too small to see one by one. Scientists group plants by how they make new plants: mosses and ferns make spores, conifers make seeds on cones, and flowering plants make seeds inside fruits. Your child tests how far spores and seeds travel in moving air, builds a key and a family tree of plant groups, and meets what botanists still argue about, such as where flowers came from.
summary.art: A wet wall in the monsoon with green moss and a small fern in a crack, a deodar branch with a cone, and a hibiscus flower, each with a small label: spores, seeds on a cone, seeds in a fruit.

intro.hook: Look under the leaf of a fern, if you can find one in a pot or on an old wall. You may see rows of brown dots. A fern never makes a flower, a fruit or a seed. So how does a new fern grow?
intro.text: The brown dots are packets of spores. A spore is a single cell, much smaller than a grain of sugar. When the packets dry, they burst and throw the spores into the air. If one lands somewhere damp, a new fern can grow. Mosses do the same. Pine trees and deodars make seeds, but on cones, not in fruits. Most plants you know, from rice to the neem tree, make seeds inside fruits. In this unit you find out why these differences matter so much that scientists use them to group all plants.
intro.art: A child's hand turning over a fern leaf to show neat rows of brown dots underneath.

outcomes: By the end I can say how flowering plants, conifers, ferns and mosses make new plants, and give an Indian example of each.
By the end I can explain how a spore differs from a seed, using the results of my fan test.
By the end I can sort plants with a key of yes-or-no questions, and make a key of my own.
By the end I can explain why mosses stay small and live in damp places, and why seeds and pollen let plants live in dry places.
By the end I can read and draw a family tree of plant groups, and say how scientists use body features and DNA to group plants.
By the end I can say what botanists still argue about, such as where flowers came from, and whether 'lower plants' is a fair name.
By the end I can design a fair test of my own and show the results in a bar chart.

terms.meaning: A plant that makes flowers. The flower makes seeds, and the seeds grow inside a fruit. Botanists call these plants angiosperms, which means 'seeds in a vessel'.
terms.example: Rice, tulsi, the coconut palm and the neem tree are all flowering plants. So is the grass on a lawn.
terms.art: A rice plant with tiny flowers on their head of grain, beside a split mango with its seed inside.

terms.meaning: A plant that never makes flowers. Some non-flowering plants make seeds on cones. Others make spores instead of seeds.
terms.example: A deodar tree, a fern and a moss are all non-flowering plants.
terms.art: Three plants side by side: a small pine with cones, a fern and a cushion of moss.

terms.meaning: A spore is one single cell that can grow into a new plant. Spores are far too small to see one by one, and carry almost no food. Ferns and mosses make spores.
terms.example: The brown dust that falls from the dots under a fern leaf is millions of spores.
terms.art: A magnified view of a few round fern spores next to a grain of sugar for size.

terms.meaning: A seed holds a tiny young plant and a store of food, wrapped in a tough coat. A seed is made of many cells, so seeds are much bigger and heavier than a spore.
terms.example: Split a soaked rajma bean, and you can see the tiny young plant lying between the two halves of food.
terms.art: A soaked rajma bean split open, with the tiny young plant inside labelled.

terms.meaning: A tree or shrub that makes seeds on cones, not inside fruits. Most conifers have narrow, needle-shaped or scale-shaped leaves that stay green all year.
terms.example: Deodar and chir pine in the Himalayas and the Khasi pine around Shillong are conifers.
terms.art: A deodar branch with needle leaves and an upright barrel-shaped cone.

terms.meaning: A cone is a woody or soft part made of many scales. Female cones hold seeds on their scales. Smaller male cones make pollen.
terms.example: A brown pine cone on the ground in Kodaikanal or Shimla has held seeds under each of its scales.
terms.art: A pine cone with one scale pulled back to show two winged seeds sitting on it.

terms.meaning: A seed that is not inside a fruit. Conifers and cycads have naked seeds. Botanists call these plants gymnosperms, which means 'naked seeds'.
terms.example: A chilgoza pine nut from a dry fruit shop is a naked seed, taken from the scale of a pine cone.
terms.art: A few long chilgoza pine nuts beside the cone scale they came from.

terms.meaning: A plant with veins and leaves, often feathery, that makes spores instead of seeds. A fern's leaf is called a frond. A young frond is rolled up like the head of a violin.
terms.example: Maidenhair fern grows on damp walls, and the ladder fern grows in cracks of old buildings in many Indian cities.
terms.art: A fern with one fully open frond and one tightly curled young frond.

terms.meaning: A brown dot under a fern frond. Each sorus is a cluster of tiny spore cases.
terms.example: Turn over a fern frond in a nursery pot, and you may see sori in neat rows.
terms.art: The underside of a fern frond with two rows of brown dots, one dot magnified to show tiny round spore cases.

terms.meaning: A small, soft green plant that grows in a carpet or cushion in damp places. Mosses have no roots and no stiff veins. They make spores in small capsules on thin stalks.
terms.example: The green velvet that grows on walls and steps in Mumbai and Kerala in the monsoon is mostly moss.
terms.art: A close-up of a moss cushion with thin stalks rising from the moss, each ending in a small capsule.

terms.meaning: Thin threads that hold a moss to a wall or the soil. They grip, but they do not carry water up the plant the way roots and veins do.
terms.example: Peel a small patch of moss off a wet brick, and you see brown threads underneath. Those are rhizoids.
terms.art: A patch of moss lifted from a brick, with fine brown threads hanging below.

terms.meaning: Long tubes inside a plant that carry water up from the roots and food around the plant. Their walls are stiffened by a tough material called lignin, so veins also hold a plant up. Ferns, conifers and flowering plants have veins. Mosses do not.
terms.example: Hold a leaf up to the light, and you can see its veins as fine lines.
terms.art: A leaf held up against a sunny window with its network of veins showing.

terms.meaning: Fine powder made by flowers and by male cones. Each grain carries the male cells a seed plant needs to make seeds. Pollen travels by wind or on animals, so it needs no water to move.
terms.example: Tap a ripe hibiscus flower over dark paper, and yellow powder falls out. A pine's small male cones in spring shed it too.
terms.art: Yellow pollen drifting from a small male pine cone onto dark paper.

terms.meaning: Sorting living things into groups. Today botanists try to make each group a family of relatives that share one ancestor.
terms.example: Rice, wheat, bamboo and lawn grass are in one family, the grass family, because they share an ancestor.
terms.art: A tree diagram with the four big plant groups on the branches.

terms.meaning: A list of yes-or-no questions that leads you, step by step, to the name or group of a living thing.
terms.example: First question: does the plant have flowers? If no, does the plant have cones? If no, does the plant have veins?
terms.art: A flow chart of yes and no arrows leading to pictures of a moss, a fern, a pine and a hibiscus.

terms.meaning: A drawing that shows which groups of plants share an ancestor. Groups on nearby branches are close relatives. Scientists call it a phylogenetic tree.
terms.example: On the tree, conifers and flowering plants sit on one branch, because both make seeds.
terms.art: A branching tree with a green alga at the root and mosses, ferns, conifers and flowering plants at the tips.

explanations.concept: The four big groups of land plants
explanations.definition: Land plants fall into four big groups by how they make new plants and whether they have veins. Mosses (and their relatives the liverworts and hornworts) have no stiff veins and make spores. Ferns have veins and make spores. Conifers and cycads have veins and make naked seeds on cones. Flowering plants have veins and make seeds inside fruits.
explanations.description: A key with three questions sorts almost any plant. Does the plant have flowers? Then the plant is a flowering plant. If not, does it make cones? Then the plant is probably a conifer or a cycad. If not, does it have veins? Then the plant is a fern. Small, soft and without veins? Then the plant is a moss or one of their relatives. The groups are not equal in size. About 9 in every 10 kinds of plant alive today are flowering plants. There are about 12,000 kinds of moss, about 10,500 kinds of fern and only about 600 kinds of conifer.
examples: Flowering: tulsi, rice, lotus, the banyan tree (their tiny flowers are hidden inside the figs)
Conifers and cycads: deodar, chir pine, the Khasi pine, the 'Christmas tree' (Araucaria) in many building gardens, and the cycad palm-like plant in hotel gardens
Ferns: maidenhair fern on wet walls, Azolla floating on rice fields, the dhekia fern eaten as a vegetable in Assam
Mosses and relatives: the green velvet on monsoon walls, and the flat green liverwort Marchantia that grows on wet nursery pots
explanations.art: Four panels: moss on a wall, a fern frond with brown dots, a pine branch with cones, and a mango tree in flower and fruit.

explanations.definition: A spore is one cell with almost no stored food. A seed is made of many cells: a tiny young plant, a store of food and a protective coat.
explanations.description: Because a spore is so small and light, gentle wind can carry spores a long way, even across seas. A fern can release millions of spores in a year, and most land where they cannot grow. A seed is heavier, so wind carries most seeds only a short way unless they have wings or hairs. But a seed carries food, so the young plant can push out a root and a shoot before they can make their own food. A seed can also wait, dry and alive, for months or years until rain comes. That is why seed plants could spread into dry lands. Orchids are flowering plants with seeds as fine as dust and almost no food. They travel far like spores, and to sprout they need help from a fungus that feeds them.
examples: In the fan test, haldi powder, as fine as spores, drifted far. Mustard seeds fell close, and the rajma dropped almost straight down.
A coconut is a huge seed with a big food store. Coconuts travel by floating on the sea, not by wind.
Aak (madar) seeds are light and have silky hairs, so the wind carries them far even though they are seeds.
explanations.art: A scale picture: a fern spore as a dot, a mustard seed, a rajma bean and a coconut, each labelled with what they carry.

explanations.concept: Why mosses stay small and damp
explanations.definition: Mosses have no veins with stiff lignin walls, and their sperm cells must swim through a film of water to reach an egg. So mosses stay small and live where they are often wet.
explanations.description: In a tree, water climbs inside narrow tubes with stiff walls. A moss has no such tubes. Water moves over a moss's surface and between their tiny leaves, the way water creeps up a cloth. That works only over a few centimetres, so most mosses stay a few centimetres tall. To make a new moss, a male cell must swim to an egg. A male cell can only swim through water, such as rain or dew. Ferns have veins, so they can grow tall, but their sperm must swim too, on a tiny heart-shaped plant that grows from a spore. Seed plants solved this problem with pollen. Wind or animals carry pollen to the egg, so no water is needed. Mosses are not helpless in dry weather, though. Many mosses sense drying, shut down and wait. When rain comes, they turn green again within hours.
examples: In the Mumbai monsoon, walls turn green with moss. In April, the same moss looks brown and dry, and turns green again with the first rain.
Ferns grow tall in the wet forests of the Western Ghats, where tree ferns can be several metres high.
A deodar can grow 50 metres tall on a dry Himalayan slope, because its veins carry water up and its pollen travels by wind.

perspectives.explanation: A moss reviving after rain is a set of chemical responses in their cells. They prefer not to call it sensing or deciding.
A moss senses drying, prepares for dry days and recovers when water returns. That is sensing and responding, which is what a mind does in every living being.

explanations.art: A moss cushion in two halves: one brown and curled in the sun, the other green and open after rain.

explanations.definition: Botanists group plants so that each group is a family of relatives, all coming from one shared ancestor. They use body features, such as veins, seeds and flowers, and, since the 1990s, the plant's DNA.
explanations.description: You could sort plants by colour, by height or by use, and every way would give different groups. But only one way finds relatives: features that were passed down from a shared ancestor. Seeds appeared once, in one group of plants, and all seed plants are their descendants. So all seed plants form one branch of the family tree. Inside that branch, flowers appeared once, and every flowering plant shares that ancestor. DNA tests mostly agree with these groups. A family tree drawn from features can be checked with a family tree drawn from DNA. When they disagree, scientists look again at both.
examples: Seeds group a deodar and a mango together, though one has needles and the other has broad leaves.
A banana plant and rice look nothing alike, but DNA and flower features show both are in the same large group of flowering plants, the monocots.
Azolla, a tiny floating plant, looks nothing like a tall fern, but her spores and DNA show she is a fern.
explanations.art: Two family trees side by side, one drawn from features and one from DNA, matching branch for branch.

explanations.concept: Where did flowering plants come from?
explanations.description: Flowering plants appear in fossils suddenly, about 130 million years ago, and within a few tens of millions of years they were everywhere. In 1879 Charles Darwin called this sudden rise 'an abominable mystery', meaning a hateful puzzle. Botanists still argue about it.
examples: The oldest flower fossils, such as Archaefructus from China, are about 125 million years old.
Fossil pollen from flowering plants goes back about 135 million years.
Amborella, a small shrub found only on the island of New Caledonia, sits on the oldest living branch of the flowering plants.

perspectives.explanation: Flowering plants began not long before their oldest fossils, about 140 million years ago, and spread fast because flowers and fruits work so well with insects and other animals.
By measuring how fast DNA changes, they estimate that flowering plants began much earlier, perhaps more than 200 million years ago, and stayed rare and small at first, so they left few fossils.
Both may be partly right: flowering plants may have begun early but spread only when insects, climate and soils changed.

explanations.art: A timeline with a gap marked 'a question mark' between the first seed plants and the first flower fossils.

explanations.description: Older textbooks called mosses and ferns 'lower plants' and flowering plants 'higher plants', as if plants climbed a ladder. Most botanists today reject this ladder. Mosses and ferns alive today have been changing for as long as flowering plants have.
examples: Mosses live on every continent, including Antarctica, where few flowering plants can survive.
Sphagnum moss holds about 20 times their own dry weight of water. Peat bogs, built mostly from dead sphagnum, store more carbon than all the trees in the world's forests.
Ferns kept spreading long after flowering plants arrived. Many fern groups alive today began in the shade of flowering forests.

perspectives.explanation: Mosses and ferns came first, and seed plants and flowers were added later, so 'lower' and 'higher' simply show the order in which the groups appeared.
Every plant alive today has an equally long history. A moss is not an unfinished fern. Each group is very good at living in its own way, so 'lower' is a misleading word.

explanations.art: A ladder crossed out, and next to it a branching bush with a moss, a fern, a pine and a lotus all at the tips of branches.

agreed.text: All land plants share one ancestor, a green alga that lived in fresh water more than 470 million years ago.
agreed.evidence: Land plants share a set of features and DNA with one group of green algae, the charophytes. The oldest spore fossils from land plants are about 470 million years old.

agreed.text: Mosses and ferns make spores, and seed plants make seeds.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see sori under a fern frond and capsules on a moss. Botanists have grown ferns and mosses from spores in the lab for over 150 years.

agreed.text: Ferns, conifers and flowering plants have veins with lignin. Mosses do not.
agreed.evidence: Thin slices looked at under a microscope show stiff water-carrying tubes in ferns and seed plants, and none of these in mosses.

agreed.text: Seed plants first appeared about 365 million years ago, and flowering plants are much younger.
agreed.evidence: The oldest true seeds are found in rocks about 365 million years old. Pollen of flowering plants appears in rocks only from about 135 million years ago.

agreed.text: About 9 in every 10 kinds of plant alive today are flowering plants.
agreed.evidence: Botanists have named about 295,000 flowering plants, compared with about 12,000 mosses, about 10,500 ferns and about 1,000 conifers, cycads and their relatives together.

challenging.who: A common belief in Europe for hundreds of years
challenging.for: New ferns appeared everywhere, but nobody could find their flowers or seeds. Some people said fern seed could make a person invisible.
challenging.against: In the 1800s, botanists watched spores fall from the sori, grow into tiny heart-shaped plants, and then into new ferns. There is no seed at all.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief that ferns had seeds you could not see.

challenging.claim: Mosses, liverworts and hornworts form one natural family of relatives.
challenging.who: Many botanists, using DNA studies since about 2018
challenging.for: Large DNA studies now mostly place these three groups together on one branch, next to the branch with all the plants that have veins.
challenging.against: For decades, other DNA studies placed them as separate steps, one after another, below the plants with veins. Some scientists still think the question is not fully settled.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the small plants without veins are one family or three separate ones.

challenging.claim: Glossopteris fossils show that India, Africa, South America, Antarctica and Australia were once joined.
challenging.who: Alfred Wegener (1915), and many geologists later
challenging.for: Glossopteris was a seed plant with tongue-shaped leaves. Their fossils are found in India, Africa, South America, Antarctica and Australia. Their seeds were too heavy to cross oceans.
challenging.against: For about 40 years, most geologists rejected the idea, because nobody knew how continents could move. In the 1960s, sea-floor studies showed how. Today this is accepted.
challenging.context: This card is about a plant fossil that helped show the continents have moved.

challenging.claim: Selaginella bryopteris, a small spore plant from India, is the Sanjeevani herb of the Ramayana.
challenging.who: Some scientists and many people in India
challenging.for: This plant curls up and looks dead when dry, and turns green again within hours of being watered. That fits a herb that brings life back.
challenging.against: The old texts describe Sanjeevani in words that could fit many plants, and scholars disagree about which plant was meant. There is no way to check.
challenging.context: This card is about a real Indian 'resurrection plant' and an old story.

challenging.claim: Seaweeds and other algae are plants.
challenging.for: Green algae make food from sunlight like plants, and land plants came from green algae.
challenging.against: Many botanists now call only land plants 'plants'. Red and brown seaweeds are on very different branches of the tree of life, so they are not close relatives of plants at all.
challenging.context: This card is about where the plant family ends.

big_questions.q: A spore is one cell, and a fern is millions of cells. How can one tiny cell know how to build a whole fern?
big_questions.hint: Think about what every cell carries inside, which the parent plant passed on.

big_questions.q: If we sort plants by colour, by use or by family, we get different groups. Which groups are real, and which are made by us?
big_questions.hint: Try sorting the same six plants three ways. Which way would a plant agree with?

big_questions.q: Mosses lived on land long before any flower. Why are they still here, if flowering plants are so successful?
big_questions.hint: Think of a place where a flowering plant could not live, but a moss could.

big_questions.q: The coal burned in India's power stations was once a forest of seed plants without flowers. When we burn coal, what are we really burning?
big_questions.hint: Where did those plants get the energy they stored in their wood?

big_questions.q: A fern throws their spores into the wind, and almost all of them land where they cannot grow. Is that waste, or is it a good way to live?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many tries a fern needs to find one damp wall.

story.title: The Brown Dust
story.note: Everything about the plants is true: fern spores, the heart-shaped plant that grows from a spore, pine cones closing in damp air, moss capsules and the old European belief in invisible fern seed. Nila, Arjun, Kamala Paati and their visit to Kodaikanal are made up.
text: Every May, Nila and her cousin Arjun went to stay with Kamala Paati in Kodaikanal. Paati had taught botany at a college for thirty years. Now she grew ferns along the stone wall of her garden, and moss grew between the steps whether she wanted it or not. Nila was ten. Arjun was eight, and he had a plan.
"I want a fern for my room in Chennai," he said on the first morning. "Paati, where are the fern seeds? I'll plant them in a pot."
Paati smiled and went on pouring filter coffee. "Look for them yourself," she said. "Nila, help him."

The children went out to the wall. The ferns were tall and feathery, and the young leaves were curled up tight, like the head of a violin. Arjun looked at the top of every leaf. He looked at the stems. He even dug a little at the roots. "There are no flowers," he said. "So there can't be any fruits. So where are the seeds?"
Nila turned a leaf over. Underneath, in two neat rows, were dozens of brown dots. "Is the fern sick?" Arjun asked. "Maybe they have some disease."

"The fern doesn't look sick," Nila said. "The dots are in rows. A disease would be messy." She picked one old leaf, the one with the darkest dots, and carried it inside. She laid it on a sheet of white paper, dots facing down, and turned a steel bowl upside down over it. "Let's see what happens by tomorrow," she said.

That evening Paati told them a story. "In Europe, hundreds of years ago, people had the same question as Arjun," she said. "Ferns spread everywhere, but no one ever saw a fern seed. So people decided the seed must be invisible. Some said that catching fern seed on one special night would make you invisible too. Even Shakespeare wrote a joke about it in one of his plays."
"Did it work?" asked Arjun.
"Nobody ever caught any," said Paati. "Because there was nothing to catch."

The next morning Nila lifted the bowl. Under the leaf, on the white paper, lay a fine brown pattern. It was the exact shape of the rows of dots, drawn in brown dust. Arjun touched it with a finger, and the dust smeared like cocoa powder. "The leaf printed itself," he said.

Paati brought her old hand lens. Through the lens, the dust was still just dust, a little grainy. "Each dot under the leaf is a bunch of tiny cases," she said. "When the air is dry, the cases split open and fling out spores. A spore is one single cell. This little heap is probably thousands of them. Each one could grow into a fern."
"So the invisible seed was real!" said Arjun.
"Almost," said Nila slowly. "But this isn't a seed. A rajma has a baby plant and food packed inside. A spore is just one cell, light enough to blow away."

Paati looked pleased. "Good. A seed is like a full tiffin box with a small passenger inside. A spore is a passenger with no tiffin at all. So the spore must land somewhere damp and start making food almost at once."

That afternoon they walked through the pine forest near the town. In the morning there had been mist, and the cones lying on the ground were shut tight. Now the sun was out, and Arjun found a cone with every scale bent open. When he shook it, a small seed with a papery wing spun down to the path.
"Pines have seeds, then," he said. "But no flowers."

"No flowers and no fruits," said Paati. "The seed sits naked on the scale of the cone. The cone opens in dry air, so the winged seeds can fly. In wet air the scales close again, and the seeds stay in." Nila took two cones home, one to keep dry and one to soak in a bucket, to see whether Paati was right. By bedtime, the soaked cone had closed.

On the last evening, Nila sat on the garden steps and looked at the moss between the stones. Rising out of the green were hundreds of thin brown stalks, each with a tiny capsule at the top, like a matchstick head. "Spores again?" she asked.

"Spores again," said Paati. "But a moss is different from a fern. A moss has no veins, the tubes that carry water up a stem. So moss stays small, and lives where the ground is wet. And to make a new moss, the moss needs rain. A male cell has to swim through a film of water to reach the egg."
"And pines don't need rain for that, because of pollen," said Nila. "The wind carries it."
"Now you know why botanists sort plants the way they do," said Paati. "Not by colour, not by size. By how they make new plants."

Arjun carried the paper with the brown print all the way home to Chennai in a closed box. With Nila's help, he tipped the dust onto damp soil in a clay pot and covered the pot with a sheet of glass. For weeks nothing happened. Then a faint green film appeared. When Nila looked closely, she saw tiny flat green hearts, smaller than a fingernail. Paati said each heart was a little plant grown from a spore, and that underneath, a male cell swims through a drop of water to an egg. Some months later, out of one of the hearts, a real fern leaf began to uncurl.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the brown dots under a fern leaf are sori, clusters of spore cases. A spore is a single cell with almost no food, which is why spores are so light and why ferns needed no seed. A spore grows first into a tiny flat heart-shaped plant, the prothallus. On it, male cells swim through water to an egg, and the young fern grows from there. Pine seeds sit naked on cone scales, and the cones open in dry air and close in damp air. Mosses have no veins and need water for their male cells to swim, so they stay small and live in damp places.
ask: Why did Arjun think the fern was sick? How did Nila work out that the fern was not?
What was the brown dust on the white paper?
Paati said a seed is like a full tiffin box with a passenger, and a spore is a passenger with none. What did she mean?
Why did the pine cones open in the sun and stay shut in the morning mist?
Why did it take so long for Arjun's fern to grow, and why did a heart shape grow first?

roots.context: We have learned how mosses, ferns, conifers and flowering plants make new plants, and how scientists group them. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the fan test, the haldi dust drifted far, but the mustard seeds dropped close to the fan. A fern's spore is one tiny cell, so the wind carries spores far. A seed holds a young plant and a food store, so seeds are heavier and land nearer. In moving air, the lighter a plant's young are, the farther they travel, and the less food they carry.
deep_truth.habit: We call mosses and ferns 'lower plants', as if a spore were a failed seed. But spores and seeds are two different bargains. Spores travel far and cost the parent little each. Seeds travel less far but start their life fed. Neither is the better way everywhere.
deep_truth.evidence: In the fan test, haldi as fine as spores spread across the paper track, while mustard fell within a short distance and rajma almost straight down. Orchid seeds, as fine as dust and with almost no food, also travel far, and they need a fungus to feed them before they can sprout.

three.who_am_i: You started as one cell too, like a spore. But you were fed by your mother for nine months, more like a seed.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings send their young out into the world. Plants do it in different ways: many light travellers, or a few well-fed ones.
three.what_is_this_world: The air around you carries spores from ferns, mosses and fungi, too small to see. Some of them came from far away.

roots.thread: All land plants came from one kind of green alga, living in fresh water more than 470 million years ago. From that one ancestor came mosses, then plants with veins, then seed plants, then flowering plants. Each new branch kept going alongside the old ones. So the one green ancestor became the many plants around you, from the moss on a wall to the rice on your plate. They are all one family, living in different ways.

teachings.source: Rig Veda 10.97.15, the hymn to plants (Oshadhi Sukta)
teachings.teaching: The hymn speaks of plants that bear fruit and plants that bear none, plants without flowers and plants with flowers.
teachings.link: More than 3,000 years ago, people in India already noticed that some plants flower and fruit and others never do. Botanists today still use flowers, fruits and seeds to group plants.

teachings.source: Jain teaching of anekantavada, many-sidedness, and the story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Each blind man touched one part of an elephant and described a different animal. Each was partly right. Only by putting the parts together did they find the whole elephant.
teachings.link: Sorting plants by colour, by height or by use each shows one side of them. Body features and DNA together give the fullest picture of who is related to whom.

science.text: All land plants share one ancestor among the green algae.
DNA studies now mostly place mosses, liverworts and hornworts together on one branch.
Why flowering plants spread so fast, about 130 million years ago, is still not fully understood.

other_view.view: The family tree of plants is real, because plants really do have ancestors. But where we cut that tree into named groups is our choice. Nature does not label her branches 'fern' or 'moss'. People do.

practice.title: Watch the spores in a sunbeam
practice.say: Let's make the room a little dark and let one beam of sunlight in. Look at the tiny specks floating in the beam. Most are dust and fibres. The air also carries spores, but each one is too small for us to see. Let's breathe slowly six times and watch the specks. Each spore is a single cell, waiting for somewhere damp.
practice.kid: Close the curtain a little. Let one sunbeam in. Watch the specks floating in it. Most are dust. Spores float in the air too, but they are too small to see. Breathe slowly six times.

ask: A spore travels far but has no food. A seed has food but stays near. If you were a plant, which would you choose, and why?
If spores are floating in your room right now, why don't ferns grow on your table?
Are the plant groups real, or are they names people made? Can they be both?

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, plant side up.

When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.

flow.parent: A good reason names a feature: brown dots under the leaves, cones, flowers or fruits. 'Because the plant is green' is not a reason, so ask for one more clue.

flow.kid: Count your cards. Which plant surprised you most? Why?

check.q: Cycas looks like a short palm. Which group is Cycas in?

Cones, because Cycas makes big cones

check.why: Cycas makes big cones and naked seeds, so they are in the cone group. They only look like a palm. A real palm, like the coconut, makes flowers and fruits.

rules: Lay all 16 cards face up so everyone can see them.
One player, the chooser, secretly picks one plant and writes the name on a slip of paper.
The others take turns asking yes-or-no questions about features only, such as 'Does the plant have cones?'. Questions about names are not allowed.
After each answer, turn face down every card that no longer fits.
Count the questions. When one card is left, the chooser shows the slip. Fewest questions wins the round. Take turns being the chooser.

setup.art: Sixteen plant cards laid face up in four rows on a floor mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out all 16 cards face up.

setup.art: A girl turning over the cards of all the flowering plants after the answer 'no' to 'Does the plant have flowers?'.
setup.caption: 2. After each answer, turn over the cards that no longer fit.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Lay them face up in four rows. 3. Choose who will be the chooser first.
flow.say: This game works like a key. Each yes-or-no question should cut the cards into two groups.
flow.kid: Lay out all 16 cards. Pick who chooses first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Twenty Questions with a Key. Here you lay out the plant cards.

flow.do: 1. The chooser picks a card in secret. 2. The others ask feature questions. 3. Turn over cards that no longer fit after each answer.
flow.say: Which question would cut the cards into two halves? A good question rules out lots of cards at once.
flow.kid: Ask a yes-or-no question about a feature. Turn over the cards that don't fit.

ask.q: Why is 'Does the plant make seeds?' a better first question than 'Is the plant a lotus?'
good: It rules out about half the cards at once.
Asking about one plant rules out only one card if the answer is no.

flow.parent: The best first questions split the cards about in half, as 'Does the plant make seeds?' does (9 cards say yes, 7 say no). Point out that this is exactly how botanists build a key.
flow.context: This is the main part of Twenty Questions with a Key. Here you ask yes-or-no questions to find the secret plant.

flow.do: 1. Count the questions in your best round. 2. Halve 16 again and again until you reach 1, and count the halvings.
flow.say: Each good question cuts the cards in half. How many halvings does it take to get from 16 cards to one?
flow.kid: Count the questions in your best round. Halve 16 until you reach 1. How many halvings was that?

check.q: Every question cuts the cards exactly in half. What is the fewest yes-or-no questions that always finds one card out of 16?
check.why: 16 halves to 8, then 4, then 2, then 1. That is 4 questions. In real life a question rarely splits the cards exactly in half, so a real key often needs more.

flow.context: This is the last step of Twenty Questions with a Key. Here you turn your best questions into a key.

experiments.title: The Fan Test: do spores or seeds travel farther?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop haldi powder, which is about as fine as fern spores, and three kinds of seed in front of a fan. Then you measure how far each one travels.
experiments.question: In moving air, which travels farther: fine dust like spores, or seeds? And does the size of the seed matter?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will drop haldi powder, mustard seeds and a rajma bean in front of a fan. Which will land farthest from where you dropped them? Which will land closest? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Drop everything from the same height, level with the middle of the fan, at the same spot just in front of it. Keep the fan at the same speed and in the same place. Only the thing you drop changes. Drop each one 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a table fan or a pedestal fan, standing on a table or stool and blowing straight across the room
haldi (turmeric) powder
mustard seeds (rai or kadugu)
dry rajma beans or kabuli chana
sheets of white paper or old notebook pages, laid end to end
a measuring tape or a 30 cm ruler, and a pencil
one more thing of your own choice to test, such as til (sesame), jeera, sooji or a small wisp of cotton

experiments.safety: Use only a pinch of haldi, and the fan's lowest speed. Keep faces out of the powder cloud, and never blow powder at anyone. Haldi stains clothes and floors, so keep it on the paper.

schedule.what: Lay the paper track. Drop each thing 3 times in front of the fan. Measure, find the averages and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, then draw a bar chart with one bar for each thing you dropped. Write one sentence for your claim, one for your evidence and one for your reasoning.

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A table fan on the floor at one end of a long line of white paper sheets, with pencil marks every 25 cm along the edge.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a paper track on the floor in front of the fan and mark every 25 cm.

setup.caption: 2. Drop each thing from the same height, just in front of the fan.

flow.do: 1. Put the fan on a table or stool at one end of a clear floor, blowing straight across the room. 2. Lay the sheets of paper end to end on the floor in a straight line, about 2.5 metres long. Start under the spot 30 cm in front of the fan. 3. With the pencil, mark the edge of the paper every 25 cm from the start. 4. Set the fan to its lowest speed.
flow.say: Today we test how far the wind can carry tiny things and bigger things. First, let's make a track to measure along.
flow.kid: Put the fan on a table, blowing across the room. Lay the paper in a long line on the floor. Mark every 25 cm with a pencil. Set the fan to slow.
flow.parent: The drop spot is about 30 cm in front of the fan, level with its middle. The air must flow past the falling things, so drop from that height, not from near the floor. Close windows, so the room's air stays still apart from the fan.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fan Test. Here you set up a paper track in front of a fan, so you can measure how far things travel.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the haldi, the mustard and the rajma. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason for each. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Which of these will travel farthest in the wind from the fan? Which will land closest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the haldi, the mustard and the rajma. Which will go farthest? Why? Write your guess.

good: The haldi is lighter, so the wind can push it more easily.
The rajma is heavy, so the bean falls fast before the wind can push them.

flow.context: This step of the Fan Test is for guessing. You guess which thing will travel farthest in the wind, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Hold one rajma bean level with the middle of the fan, at the drop spot. 2. Let go without throwing. 3. Measure where the bean first landed, before rolling, if you can see. 4. Do this 3 times and write each distance in the table.
flow.say: Hold your hand at the drop spot, level with the middle of the fan. Just open your fingers. Don't throw.
flow.kid: Hold one rajma at the drop spot, level with the fan's middle. Let go. Where did it land? Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: If a bean rolls, measure where the bean first hit the paper. Watching carefully is part of the test.
flow.context: This step of the Fan Test drops the biggest seed, a rajma bean, in front of the fan and measures how far it lands.

flow.do: 1. Hold 3 or 4 mustard seeds at the same height. 2. Let them fall. 3. Measure to the seed that landed farthest. 4. Do this 3 times and write each distance in the table.
flow.say: Now the mustard seeds. Same height, same spot. Watch where they land.
flow.kid: Drop a few mustard seeds from the same height. Find the one that went farthest. Measure. Do it 3 times.
flow.context: This step of the Fan Test drops small seeds, mustard, in front of the fan and measures how far they travel.

flow.do: 1. Take a small pinch of haldi between your finger and thumb. 2. Hold it at the same height and rub your fingers gently, so it falls as a cloud. 3. Wait until the cloud settles, about one minute. 4. Look along the paper for the farthest yellow you can see, and measure. 5. Do this 3 times.
flow.say: Haldi powder is about as fine as fern spores. Let's see where the wind takes it. Keep your face away from the cloud.
flow.kid: Take a tiny pinch of haldi. Rub your fingers so it falls as a cloud. Keep your face away. Wait a minute. Find the farthest yellow. Measure.

ask.q: What did the haldi do that the seeds did not?
good: It floated in the air for a while.
It spread out along the paper instead of landing in one spot.
Some of it went past the end of the track.

flow.parent: Some haldi may float past the end of the track. If so, write 'more than 250 cm'. The faint yellow is easier to see if you look along the paper from low down, near the floor.
flow.context: This step of the Fan Test drops fine haldi powder, a model for fern spores, in front of the fan and measures how far it drifts.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to choose one more thing to test, such as til, jeera, sooji or a wisp of cotton. 2. Ask them to predict where it fits among the three results. 3. Test it 3 times in the same way.
flow.say: Now you design part of the test. Choose one more thing. Where do you think it will land, compared with the others? Why?
flow.kid: Choose one more thing to test. Guess where it will land. Say why. Test it 3 times.
flow.parent: This is your child's own investigation. Ask them which things must stay the same for it to be fair: the height, the spot and the fan speed.
flow.context: This step of the Fan Test lets you choose and test one more thing, to see whether it fits the pattern.

flow.do: 1. Work out the average for each thing: add the three distances and divide by 3. 2. Draw a bar chart. 3. Say a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
flow.say: What did we find? Tell me your claim, the evidence from our numbers, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Add your three numbers. Divide by 3. Draw a bar for each thing. Say what you found and why.

ask.q: A fern spore is about as fine as haldi. What does our test tell us about how ferns spread?
good: The wind can carry fern spores far away.
That is how ferns can appear on a wall far from any other fern.

ask.q: A seed is heavier than a spore. What does a seed have that a spore does not?
good: A young plant and a store of food inside.
A tough coat.

check.q: In the Fan Test, why did the haldi travel much farther than the rajma?
options: Haldi is yellow, and yellow things float
Each grain of haldi is so light that moving air can carry it before it falls
The rajma was dropped from lower down
check.why: Tiny, light grains fall very slowly, so moving air has time to carry them far. A rajma is heavy and falls fast. Colour has nothing to do with it. And in a fair test, everything was dropped from the same height.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Fan Test. Here you find the averages, draw a bar chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: The Pine Cone Weather Test (if you have a pine cone)
experiments.context: In this experiment you soak a pine cone in water and then dry it, to see whether the cone opens and closes with the weather. You need a dry, open pine cone: from a hill station, a craft shop or a nursery.
experiments.question: Does a pine cone close when wet and open when dry? How does that help the pine tree?
experiments.predict: Guess first. What will happen to an open pine cone after an hour in water? What will happen when it dries in the sun again? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Measure the same cone at its widest point each time, with the same ruler. Compare it with a second cone that stays dry, so you know the change came from the water and not from time passing.

materials.item: two dry, open pine cones of about the same size
a bucket or deep bowl of water
a ruler
a sunny windowsill

schedule.what: Measure both cones. Soak one for an hour. Measure both again.
Measure the soaked cone after a day in the sun. Count the spirals on the dry cone.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the wet cone and the dry cone side by side.

setup.caption: 1. Measure both cones across their widest part.

setup.art: A pine cone sunk in a bowl of water, held down by a steel cup, and a second cone on the table beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Soak one cone. Keep the other dry.

flow.do: 1. Measure each cone across its widest part. 2. Write both widths in the table. 3. Ask for a prediction and a reason.
flow.say: What will water do to this open cone? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Measure both cones. Write the numbers. Guess what water will do. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pine Cone Weather Test. Here you measure two open pine cones and guess what water will do.

flow.do: 1. Push one cone under the water and hold it down with a cup. 2. Leave the other cone dry. 3. After one hour, take the wet cone out and measure both cones again.
flow.say: Let's leave this one in the water for an hour. The other one stays dry, so we can compare.
flow.kid: Sink one cone in water. Keep the other dry. Wait one hour. Measure both again.

ask.q: What changed? Why might a pine tree's cones close in rain?
good: The wet cone closed up.
Wet seeds can't fly well, so the cone keeps them in until it is dry.
The scales protect the seeds in rain.

flow.parent: Most cones close within one or two hours. The scales are made of two layers that swell differently when wet, so the scales bend shut. The cone is no longer growing, and it works like a hinge made by the tree.
flow.context: This step of the Pine Cone Weather Test soaks one cone for an hour and compares it with a dry one.

flow.do: 1. Put the wet cone in a sunny spot for a day. 2. Measure it again. 3. On the dry cone, count the spirals of scales going one way, then the other way.
flow.say: Has the cone opened again? Now let's count the spirals of scales. Count the ones curving left, then the ones curving right.
flow.kid: Measure the cone after a day in the sun. Count the spirals one way. Then the other way.
flow.parent: Many pine cones have 8 spirals one way and 13 the other, or 5 and 8. These are neighbouring numbers in the Fibonacci pattern, where each number is the sum of the two before it.

check.q: A pine cone opened on a dry, sunny day. Why is that a good time for a pine tree's seeds to come out?
options: Dry winged seeds fly farther in dry air
The seeds need to be warm to be eaten
Rain would wash the cone off the tree
check.why: Pine seeds have a papery wing. A dry wing spins and glides on the wind, but a wet seed is heavy and drops straight down. So opening in dry weather sends the seeds farther.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Pine Cone Weather Test. Here you see whether the soaked cone opens again, and count the spirals of scales.

experiments.title: What Comes Out of the Brown Dots? (if you can get a fern leaf)
experiments.context: In this experiment you lay a fern leaf with brown dots on white paper overnight, to see what falls out. Ferns grow in many nursery pots and building gardens, and on damp walls.
experiments.question: What are the brown dots under a fern leaf, and what comes out of them?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you leave a fern leaf with brown dots on white paper overnight, will anything appear on the paper? What will it look like, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Lay one leaf with dark brown dots and one leaf with no dots on the same kind of paper, under the same kind of bowl, for the same time. Then you can tell whether the dots made the difference.
results_table: What we saw on the paper
