setup.caption: 3. Next morning, lift the bowl and look.

flow.do: 1. Look at the brown dots with a hand lens or the phone camera. 2. Ask what your child thinks they are, and why.
flow.say: What do you think these brown dots are? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the brown dots up close. What do you think they are? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the brown dots experiment. Here you look closely at the dots under a fern leaf.

flow.do: 1. Lay each frond on white paper with the underside down. 2. Cover each with an upside-down bowl, so moving air cannot blow the dust away. 3. Leave them overnight.
flow.say: The bowl keeps the air still. Tomorrow we'll see if anything fell out.
flow.kid: Put each leaf face down on white paper. Cover it with a bowl. Leave it overnight.
flow.context: This step of the brown dots experiment sets up two fern leaves on white paper to leave overnight.

flow.do: 1. Lift the bowls and the fronds gently. 2. Compare the two papers. 3. Look at the dust with the lens.
flow.say: What do you see? Is there a difference between the two papers?
flow.kid: Lift the bowls. Lift the leaves. What is on the paper? Look with the lens.
flow.parent: Ripe dots usually leave a fine brown dust in the shape of their rows. If nothing appears, the dots may be too young or already empty. Try a leaf with darker, fuzzier dots. The spores are single cells, so even through a lens they look like fine dust.

good: Spores.
Thousands of tiny single cells that can each grow into a new fern.

check.q: A fern leaf left a brown dust print on white paper. What is the dust?
options: Seeds
Spores, each a single cell
Pollen from the fern's flowers
check.why: Ferns make spores, not seeds. A spore is one cell with almost no food. Ferns have no flowers, so the dust is not pollen.

flow.context: This is the last step of the brown dots experiment. Here you look at what fell out of the fern leaf overnight.

activities.title: Split a Dhania Seed: seed or fruit?
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at seeds from the kitchen, and find out that some 'seeds' are really whole fruits. It starts the big question of the unit: how do plants without flowers or fruits make new plants?

materials.item: whole dhania (coriander) seeds
a few mustard seeds, a rajma bean soaked in water overnight (start the evening before), and a few whole jeera
a chilgoza pine nut, if you have one
a steel plate and a clean fingernail or blunt butter knife

activities.record: Draw a whole dhania seed and the two halves.

setup.art: A steel plate with dhania, mustard, jeera and a soaked rajma bean in small heaps.
setup.caption: 1. Put a few kitchen seeds on a plate.

setup.art: Fingers pressing a round dhania seed splitting into two half-domes.
setup.caption: 2. Press a dhania seed until the seed splits in two.

flow.do: 1. Put the seeds on the plate. 2. Ask your child to press a dhania seed between finger and thumb until the seed splits. 3. Look at the two halves.
flow.say: Every one of these seeds came from a flower. Let's split a dhania seed. What do you see?
flow.kid: Press a dhania seed hard. Does it split? Look at the two halves.
flow.parent: A dhania 'seed' is really a tiny dry fruit. The 'seed' splits into two halves, and each half holds one true seed. Jeera is a fruit in the same way.
flow.context: This is the first step of Split a Dhania Seed. Here you split a coriander seed to see what is inside.

flow.do: 1. Split the soaked rajma along its middle. 2. Find the tiny young plant inside. 3. If you have a chilgoza, show that the nut came straight off a pine cone scale, with no fruit around it.
flow.say: A rajma seed grew inside a pod, which is the fruit. A chilgoza grew on a pine cone with no fruit at all.
flow.kid: Split the soft rajma. Find the tiny plant inside. A chilgoza grew on a cone, with no fruit.
flow.context: This step of Split a Dhania Seed compares a seed from a fruit with a naked seed from a pine cone.

flow.do: 1. Line up a rajma, a mustard seed and a dhania seed, biggest to smallest. 2. Say that a fern spore is far smaller than all three. Ask what it can have inside. 3. Write your child's guess to compare with the Fan Test.
flow.say: A fern spore is much smaller than the smallest of these. What could fit inside something so small, and what could not?
flow.kid: A fern spore is smaller than all of these. What could fit inside it? What could not? Write your guess.

ask.q: What could a spore not have room for?
good: A young plant and a store of food.
A tough coat made of many cells.

flow.context: This is the last step of Split a Dhania Seed. Here you ask how plants without seeds make new plants.

activities.title: A Key for the Four Plant Groups
activities.context: In this activity you use a key, a list of yes-or-no questions, to sort 16 plants into the four big groups. Then you make a different key of your own.

materials.item: the 16 plant cards from the game Twenty Questions with a Key, or 16 plant names written on slips of paper
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Draw your own key as a flow chart with yes and no arrows.

setup.art: A paper flow chart: Flowers? yes leads to Flowering plant, no leads to Cones? and so on to Fern and Moss.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the key onto a sheet of paper.

setup.art: Plant cards placed in four heaps at the ends of the key's arrows.
setup.caption: 2. Walk each plant card through the key.

flow.do: 1. Copy this key onto paper. Question 1: Does the plant make flowers? Yes means a flowering plant. 2. Question 2: Does the plant make cones? Yes means a conifer or cycad. 3. Question 3: Does the plant have veins? Yes means a fern. No means a moss or relative.
flow.say: A key is a set of questions. Each answer sends you down one arrow. Let's draw one.
flow.kid: Copy the key. Each question has a yes arrow and a no arrow.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Four-Question Key. Here you copy a key that sorts plants into four groups.

flow.do: 1. Take each plant card. 2. Start at question 1 and follow the arrows. 3. Put the card at the end of its arrow.
flow.say: Start at the top every time. Which arrow does the lotus take?
flow.kid: Take a card. Start at the top. Follow the arrows. Put the card where you end up.

ask.q: Which plant was hardest to sort, and why?
good: The banyan, because the flowers are hidden in the figs.
Cycas, because they look like a palm.

flow.context: This step of the Four-Question Key walks each plant card through the key.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to make a new key for the same plants. It should start with a different question, such as 'Does the plant make seeds?'. 2. Test it on every card. 3. Check that each plant still ends up in their group.
flow.say: Can you make a key that starts with a different question? Does the plant still sort every plant correctly?
flow.kid: Make your own key. Start with a new question. Test it on every card.
flow.parent: A strong key asks about features that every plant either has or lacks, such as seeds or veins. Questions like 'Is the plant big?' fail, because 'big' means different things to different people.

check.q: Which question is best for a key?
options: Is the plant pretty?
Does the plant make seeds?
Is the plant big?
check.why: Every plant either makes seeds or does not, so everyone gets the same answer. 'Pretty' and 'big' depend on who is looking, so two people could go down different arrows.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Four-Question Key. Here you design a key of your own and test it.

activities.title: Draw the Family Tree from Clues
activities.context: In this activity you use a table of features to draw a family tree of five living beings: a green alga, a moss, a fern, a pine and a mango tree. It shows how botanists find who is related to whom.

materials.item: paper, a pencil and colours

activities.record: Draw the nested circles and the family tree.

example_chart.title: Features of five living beings
rows: Lives on land, with a young plant protected by the parent

setup.art: Five big nested circles drawn on paper, each labelled with a feature, with a mango drawn in the smallest one.
setup.caption: 1. Draw nested circles, one for each feature.

setup.art: A branching tree drawn from the circles, with alga, moss, fern, pine and mango at the tips.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the circles into a family tree.

flow.do: 1. Read the table of features together. 2. Draw a big circle for 'makes food from sunlight' and put all five inside. 3. Inside it, draw a circle for 'lives on land'. 4. Keep drawing smaller circles for veins, seeds, then flowers.
flow.say: Each feature is a circle. Who goes inside each one?
flow.kid: Draw a big circle for 'makes food from sunlight'. Put all five inside. Draw a smaller circle for each next feature.
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Family Tree from Clues. Here you draw nested circles from a table of features.

flow.do: 1. Turn the circles into a tree: one trunk, and a branch splitting off at each new feature. 2. Put the alga on the first branch, then the moss, the fern, the pine, and the mango at the top. 3. Mark each split with the feature that appeared there.
flow.say: Each time a new feature appears, the tree splits. The plants after the split all have it.
flow.kid: Draw a trunk. Make a branch for each new feature. Put each plant on their branch.

ask.q: Which two are the closest relatives in your tree?
good: The pine and the mango, because both make seeds.
They share the most features.

flow.context: This step of Draw the Family Tree from Clues turns the circles into a branching family tree.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether the moss is the 'ancestor' of the fern. 2. Point out that the moss on your wall today is a cousin, not a grandparent.
flow.say: Is the moss alive today the great-grandmother of the fern? Or are they cousins?
flow.kid: Is today's moss the fern's grandmother? Or their cousin? Why?
flow.parent: Living mosses and living ferns share an ancestor that lived long ago, but neither came from the other. Both have kept changing since. This is why a family tree has living plants only at the tips.

check.q: On the family tree, why are the pine and the mango on one branch?
options: They both make seeds
They are both tall trees
They both live in India
check.why: Seeds appeared once, in one ancestor, and every seed plant came from that ancestor. Being tall or living in India does not show who is related to whom.

flow.context: This is the last step of Draw the Family Tree from Clues. Here you think about what the branches of the tree mean.

activities.title: Hunt for Plants Without Flowers in the City
activities.context: In this activity you look for mosses, ferns and conifers near your home: on walls, in drains, in pots and in your building's garden. They are easiest to find in or after the monsoon.

materials.item: a phone camera or a hand lens
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up comes along outside. Look at drains, but don't touch the water. Don't climb walls to reach plants.
activities.record: Make a table: what you found, where, and which group.

setup.art: A damp shaded wall at the bottom of a building, with green moss and a small fern growing from a crack.
setup.caption: 1. Look on damp, shady walls and around drains.

setup.art: A child zooming in with a phone camera on moss capsules on a wall.
setup.caption: 2. Zoom in with a phone or a lens.

setup.art: A building garden with a tall Araucaria 'Christmas tree' and a Cycas.
setup.caption: 3. Look for cone plants in the building garden.

flow.do: 1. Walk around the building with your child. 2. Look on shady walls, steps, drains, flower pots and in the garden. 3. Photograph every moss, fern or cone plant you find.
flow.say: Look in damp, shady places. Mosses and ferns need water. Cone plants are often planted in gardens.
flow.kid: Look on shady walls and steps. Look near drains and in pots. Take a photo of each one.
flow.parent: The ladder fern often grows from cracks in old walls and around drains in Indian cities. In the dry months, moss looks brown and flat, but they are still alive.
flow.context: This is the first step of the city hunt. Here you look for mosses, ferns and cone plants around your building.

flow.do: 1. At home, look at the photos together. 2. Use the key from A Key for the Four Plant Groups to sort each one. 3. Mark the places on a rough map of your building.
flow.say: Where did we find the mosses? Where did we find the cone plants? Why there?
flow.kid: Sort your photos into the groups. Mark where you found each one.

ask.q: Why were the mosses only in some places?
good: They grow where it stays wet and shady.
Their sperm needs water to swim.
They have no veins to carry water up.

flow.context: This is the last step of the city hunt. Here you sort your finds and see where each group grows.

activities.title: The Moss Sponge
activities.context: In this activity you test how much water moss holds, compared with dry soil. Use dry sphagnum moss, sold in nurseries for orchids, or a small patch of moss from a wet wall that you have let dry for two days.

materials.item: a loose pinch of dry sphagnum moss about the size of a lime, or a small patch of wall moss dried for two days
a lump of dry soil from a flower pot, loosened, about the same size
two steel tumblers, each with 200 ml of water, measured with a measuring cup or a medicine cup
a measuring cup
a small tea strainer or a thin cloth tied into a bundle

activities.record: Write how much water was left in each tumbler, and work out how much each one held.

setup.art: Two steel tumblers of water, one with a wad of moss pushed in, one with cotton wool.
setup.caption: 1. Push the moss into one tumbler and the soil into the other.

setup.art: A hand lifting the dripping moss over the tumbler.
setup.caption: 2. Lift each one out and let it drip for one minute.

flow.do: 1. Put the moss in the strainer (or cloth) and push it into one tumbler. Rinse the strainer, put the soil in it and push it into the other tumbler. 2. Wait two minutes. 3. Lift each one out and hold it over its tumbler for one minute while it drips.
flow.say: Which will hold more water, the moss or the soil? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which holds more water. Say why. Put the moss in a strainer and push it into one tumbler. Do the same with the soil. Wait. Lift each out and let it drip.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Moss Sponge. Here you soak moss and dry soil in the same amount of water.

flow.do: 1. Pour what is left in each tumbler into the measuring cup. 2. Take it away from 200 ml to find what each one held.
flow.say: If 140 ml is left, then the moss held 60 ml. Let's find out.
flow.kid: Measure what is left. Take it away from 200. That is what each one held.
flow.context: This step of the Moss Sponge measures how much water the moss and the soil held.

flow.do: 1. Compare the results. 2. Explain why moss holds water.
flow.say: Sphagnum has big empty cells in their leaves that fill with water. Why is that useful for a plant with no veins?
flow.kid: Which held more? Why might that help a moss?
flow.parent: Sphagnum leaves have large, empty, dead cells that soak up water, so sphagnum can hold about 20 times their own dry weight. A plant with no veins must keep water close.

check.q: Why is holding water useful for a moss?
options: A moss has no veins, so water must stay close to their cells
Water makes the moss heavier so the wind cannot blow them away
Mosses drink only once a year
check.why: With no veins to bring water from below, a moss must soak up and hold rain and dew around their cells.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Moss Sponge. Here you compare the results and think about why moss holds water.

activities.title: Coal from a Lost Forest: the Glossopteris map
activities.context: In this activity you fit the southern continents together like a jigsaw, and mark where fossils of Glossopteris, a seed plant without flowers, have been found. Much of India's coal formed from forests of Glossopteris and their neighbours.

materials.item: a printed or hand-traced world map
scissors, glue and a green pen

activities.record: Stick the joined continents on a page and mark the fossils.

setup.art: Paper cut-outs of India, Africa, South America, Antarctica and Australia, laid apart on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the five southern continents.

setup.art: The same cut-outs fitted together into one big land, with green tongue-shaped leaf marks across all of them.
setup.caption: 2. Fit them together and mark the Glossopteris fossils.

flow.do: 1. Cut out India, Africa, South America, Antarctica and Australia. 2. Fit them together so that India sits against Antarctica and Africa, and South America against Africa. 3. Glue them down.
flow.say: About 280 million years ago, these lands were joined in one big land called Gondwana. Let's fit them back together.
flow.kid: Cut out the five lands. Fit them together like a jigsaw. Glue them down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Glossopteris map. Here you fit five continents together into one land.

flow.do: 1. Draw small tongue-shaped leaves in green across all five lands. 2. Mark India's coalfields in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal.
flow.say: Glossopteris fossils are found on all five lands. Their seeds were too heavy to cross an ocean. What does that tell us?
flow.kid: Draw green leaves on all five lands. Mark where India's coal is.

ask.q: How could the same plant grow in India and Antarctica?
good: The lands were once joined.
The plant spread across one big land before the land split apart.

flow.parent: Much of the coal in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh formed from forests that included Glossopteris, about 250 to 300 million years ago. Their seeds were large, so they could not have crossed the sea.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Glossopteris map. Here you mark the fossils and India's coalfields.

activities.title: Are Mosses 'Lower' Plants? A Debate
activities.context: In this activity you argue both sides of a real question: are mosses and ferns 'lower plants', as old books say, or is that a misleading name?

materials.item: two sheets of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write your best point for each side, and your final view.

setup.art: A sheet of paper split into two columns: 'Lower plants' and 'Not lower'.
setup.caption: 1. Make two columns.

setup.art: A girl and her father facing each other across a table, each holding a card with arguments.
setup.caption: 2. Take a side each, then swap.

flow.do: 1. Write the two sides as headings. 2. Your child argues 'Mosses are lower plants' for two minutes. 3. You argue 'Not lower' for two minutes.
flow.say: One side says mosses came first and are simpler, so they are lower. The other says every living plant has an equally long history. Let's argue.
flow.kid: Argue one side for two minutes. Use facts from the unit. Then listen to the other side.
flow.context: This is the first step of the moss debate. Here each person argues one side.

flow.do: 1. Swap sides and argue again. 2. Each person says which side they now think is stronger, and why.
flow.say: Now swap. What is the strongest point for the side you didn't choose?
flow.kid: Swap sides. Argue again. Then say what you really think, and why.

good: Mosses live in Antarctica, where few flowering plants can.
Mosses came first in time.
Peat moss stores huge amounts of carbon.

flow.parent: A strong answer separates 'came earlier' from 'is worse'. Mosses' ancestors came earlier, but today's mosses have been changing for just as long as roses.
flow.context: This is the last step of the moss debate. Here you swap sides and decide what you think.

projects.title: The Green Jar: do spores come from the air?
projects.context: In this four-week project you test whether spores floating in the air can land on bare soil and grow. One jar of soil is open to the air for a day, and one is closed at once.

materials.item: two clear glass jars with lids, or two clear plastic boxes with lids
soil from a flower pot
materials.qty: enough to fill each jar a quarter full

materials.item: a steel bowl and a kettle of boiling water, for the grown-up
a plate to cover the bowl while the soil cools
a bright windowsill out of direct midday sun

projects.safety: A grown-up pours the boiling water into the steel bowl, not into a glass jar, because hot water can crack glass. Wait until the soil is cool. Once something grows, do not open the jars or sniff them. Mould can bother people with asthma or allergies, so look through the glass.

schedule.what: A grown-up pours boiling water over the soil in a steel bowl, covers it and lets it cool. Spoon the damp soil into both jars. Close jar B at once. Leave jar A open by the window all day, then close it.
Look at both jars through the glass, with a lens or phone zoom. Note any green or white patches.
Look again and draw what you see.
Look again. Measure any green patch.
Compare the two jars and write a conclusion.

projects.record: Draw both jars every week. Write a claim, the evidence and your reasoning at the end.

setup.art: Two jars a quarter full of soil, one open and one covered with cling film, on a bright windowsill.
setup.caption: 1. Jar A open for a day. Jar B closed at once.

setup.art: A close-up of the soil in jar A with a faint green film and tiny moss threads.
setup.caption: 2. Look every week for green or white patches.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts the soil in a steel bowl and pours boiling water over it, then covers the bowl with a plate. 2. When the soil is cool, spoon it into both jars, damp but not dripping. 3. Close jar B at once. 4. Leave jar A open by the window all day, then close it.
flow.say: The hot water kills most spores already in the soil. Then only jar A catches new spores from the air.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours hot water on the soil. Wait until it is cool. Put the soil in both jars. Close jar B. Leave jar A open all day.
flow.parent: Both jars get the same soil, water and light. Only one thing changes: whether the soil was open to the air. Boiling does not kill every spore, so a little growth in jar B is possible. Say so in the result.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Green Jar. Here you set up two jars of soil, one open to the air for a day.

flow.do: 1. Once a week, look at both jars through the glass, with a lens or phone zoom. 2. Draw what you see. 3. Do not open the jars.
flow.say: Is anything growing yet? Is it green or white?
flow.kid: Look at both jars each week, through the glass. Draw what you see. Do not open them.
flow.parent: Over 2 to 4 weeks, a green film of algae or young moss, or white fluffy mould, often appears. Mould is a fungus, which also grows from spores. If nothing grows in either jar, that is a real result too: say so.
flow.context: This step of the Green Jar is the weekly check, to see whether anything grows from spores.

flow.do: 1. Compare the jars on day 28. 2. Write a claim, the evidence and your reasoning.
flow.say: What did the open jar catch that the covered jar did not? What does that tell us about the air?
flow.kid: Compare the jars. What grew in each? What does that tell you about the air?

ask.q: Where did the green come from?
good: From spores that floated in from the air.
Moss or algae spores landed on the open soil.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Green Jar. Here you compare the two jars after four weeks.

challenges.title: A Seed That Flies and Still Carries Food
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Fan Test, the heavy rajma barely moved. Here you design wings or hairs that help a heavy seed travel farther in the same wind.
challenges.problem: Use a kabuli chana as your seed, with the food store inside. Add a design that makes the chana land as far as possible from the drop spot in front of the fan.
constraints: The chana must stay attached and must not be cut.
Use only paper, thread, tape and cotton from home.
Drop the chana from the same height and spot as in the Fan Test (level with the middle of the fan), with the fan on its lowest speed.
materials: the paper track from the Fan Test
general: Add one paper wing, like a pine seed, so the seed spins while falling.
Add a cotton tuft on top, like the silky hairs on aak (madar) seeds.
Tape the chana under a small paper parachute.
creative: Make a flat, wide paper disc that glides like a frisbee.
Try two small wings instead of one large one, and compare.
Wrap the chana in a light paper cone, like a shuttlecock.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own flying seed. Draw it, build it and test it 3 times. Did it beat the bare chana? By how many centimetres?

setup.art: A chana taped under a paper wing, beside a chana with a cotton tuft.
setup.caption: 1. Build a flying seed around a chana.

setup.art: The flying seed spinning down in front of a fan above the paper track.
setup.caption: 2. Test it on the Fan Test track.

flow.do: 1. Drop a bare chana 3 times in front of the fan. 2. Write down the average distance.
flow.say: First let's see how far a bare chana goes. That is the number to beat.
flow.kid: Drop a bare chana 3 times. Measure. That is the number to beat.
flow.context: This is the first step of the flying seed challenge. Here you measure how far a bare chana travels.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: wings, tufts and parachutes. 2. Build one design. 3. Test it 3 times and find the average.
flow.say: Pine seeds have a wing, and aak seeds have silky hairs. Which idea do you want to try first? Why?
flow.kid: Pick an idea. Build it. Test it 3 times.
flow.context: This step of the flying seed challenge builds and tests a design.

flow.do: 1. Build your own new design. 2. Test it 3 times. 3. Compare it with the bare chana.
flow.say: What made your best design work? What does that tell us about real seeds?
flow.kid: Make your own design. Test it. Did it beat the bare chana?

check.q: Why do aak seeds have silky hairs?
options: The hairs catch the wind, so the seeds fall slowly and drift far
The hairs keep the seeds warm
The hairs make the seeds taste bad
check.why: Silky hairs catch a lot of air for very little weight, so the seed falls slowly and the wind carries them away from the parent.

flow.context: This is the last step of the flying seed challenge. Here you design your own flying seed and compare.

challenges.title: A Key for a Six-Year-Old
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a picture key that a child of six, who cannot read well yet, could use to sort plants into spores, cones and flowers.
challenges.problem: Design a key with pictures and very few words. Test it with a younger child, or with a grown-up pretending not to read.
constraints: It must sort at least 8 plant cards correctly.
materials: the plant cards from Spore, Cone or Flower?
general: Use a drawing of a flower for 'Does the plant have flowers?'.
Use a drawing of a cone for 'Does the plant have cones?'.
Use a drawing of brown dots under a leaf for 'Does the plant have spore dots?'.
creative: Make the key a board game path, with a yes path and a no path.
Make it a fold-out booklet, one question per page.
Use real pressed leaves and a pine scale stuck on the card.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own picture key. Test it with someone younger. Where did they get stuck? Change that question and test again.

setup.art: A colourful picture key on a sheet of paper, with drawings of a flower, a cone and brown dots, and yes and no arrows.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a key with pictures.

setup.art: A small child pointing at the flower picture while holding a plant card.
setup.caption: 2. Test the key with a younger child.

flow.do: 1. Choose three questions. 2. Draw a picture for each. 3. Add yes and no arrows.
flow.say: A good key works for anyone. Which questions can a six-year-old answer just by looking?
flow.kid: Pick three questions. Draw a picture for each. Add yes and no arrows.
flow.context: This is the first step of the picture key challenge. Here you design a key with pictures.

flow.do: 1. Test the key with a younger child or a grown-up. 2. Watch where they get stuck. 3. Change that question and test again.
flow.say: Where did they get stuck? How can we make that question clearer?
flow.kid: Test your key with someone younger. Fix the question that was hard.

check.q: A younger child got stuck on 'Does the plant have veins?'. What is the best fix?
options: Draw a leaf held up to light with lines showing
Say the word 'veins' louder
Remove the question and guess
check.why: A picture of veins in a leaf shows what to look for. Saying the word louder does not explain it, and guessing makes the key useless.

flow.context: This is the last step of the picture key challenge. Here you test your key and improve it.

items.p: Which of these plants makes spores, not seeds?
items.why: Ferns make spores. The mango and rice make seeds in fruits, and the deodar makes seeds on cones. Choosing the deodar means thinking 'no flowers means no seeds', but conifers make seeds without flowers.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Class 5 in Pune, says, 'Every plant makes flowers at some time in their life.' Is she right?
items.why: False. Mosses, ferns and conifers never make flowers. A strong answer names one, such as a fern or a pine.

items.p: Ferns and mosses make tiny single cells called ____ instead of seeds.
items.why: A spore is one cell that can grow into a new plant. Spores carry almost no food, so they are very light.

items.p: Sort these plants into their groups.
items.a: see items
items.why: Tulsi, rice and coconut have flowers. Deodar, chir pine and Cycas make cones. Maidenhair fern and wall moss make spores. A strong answer can give the clue used for each.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give an Indian example of each.
pairs: one cell that can grow into a new fern or moss
a part with scales that holds naked seeds or makes pollen
thin threads that hold a moss to a wall
powder that carries the male cells of a seed plant

items.p: Remember the Fan Test, where you dropped haldi, mustard and rajma in front of a fan. Explain why the haldi landed farthest. Use the word 'light' or 'heavy' in your answer.
items.a: Each grain of haldi is very small and light, so it falls very slowly. The moving air from the fan has time to carry it a long way before it lands. The rajma is heavy and falls fast, so the air hardly moves the bean.
items.why: A strong answer links how slowly something falls to how far the air can carry it, and uses evidence from the test.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 5 in Kochi, sees green moss on her wall in the monsoon. In April the same moss looks brown and dry. Why?
opts: Mosses grow and stay green only when they are wet
Moss turns brown because they are old and dead
Moss is green only in the dark
items.why: Mosses have no veins to bring up water, so they need rain and damp air. In dry weather they shut down and turn brown, and they turn green again with the first rain. Choosing 'dead' means not knowing that many mosses can survive drying.

items.p: Draw the underside of a fern frond. Show the brown dots and label 'frond' and 'sorus (spore dots)'.
items.a: A frond with rows of dots underneath, labelled frond and sorus.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the dots in neat rows or lines under the leaf, not scattered like a disease.
items.art: A blank outline of a fern frond.

items.p: Three of these plants make cones. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The deodar, the chir pine and the chilgoza pine are conifers. The coconut palm is a flowering plant, and the coconut is a fruit.

items.p: Grass on a lawn is a flowering plant.
items.why: True. Grasses make small flowers without bright petals, because wind carries their pollen. Rice and wheat are grasses too, and each grain is a fruit.

items.p: Put these steps of a fair test of how far things blow in front of a fan in order.
a: Lay a paper track in front of the fan and mark it every 25 cm
Guess which will travel farthest and say why
Drop each thing 3 times from the same height
Find the averages and draw a bar chart
items.why: First set up, then predict, then test fairly, then work out the results.
items: Drop each thing 3 times from the same height
Find the averages and draw a bar chart

Guess which will travel farthest and say why

items.p: Label a drawing of a moss plant: leaves, rhizoids, stalk and spore capsule.
a: Spore capsule at the top of the stalk
items.why: A moss's spore capsule sits on a thin stalk above the leafy part. The rhizoids hold the moss to the wall.
items.art: A moss plant drawn large, with blank label lines.

items.p: Two friends in Hyderabad argue about spores and seeds.
items.a: A strong answer uses how far things blow: tiny spores travel far, heavy seeds stay near. It sees that each way has a cost: spores have no food, seeds travel less far. It agrees with one friend and gives one fair point from the other.
items.why: There is no single winner. Each way of making new plants suits a different kind of life.

views.says: Seeds are better. A seed has food inside, so the young plant gets a good start.
Spores are better. They are so light that the wind carries them far, and a fern makes millions of them.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Use what you know about how far light and heavy things blow in the wind. Then say one thing the other friend has right.

items.p: A dhania 'seed' splits into two halves when pressed. What does this show?
opts: A dhania 'seed' is really a tiny fruit with two seeds inside
items.why: Dhania is a flowering plant. What we call a seed is a small dry fruit, and each half holds one true seed. Seeds of flowering plants always form inside a fruit.

items.p: Name one plant without flowers that you might see in an Indian city. Say where you would look for them, and which group they are in.
items.a: For example: the ladder fern, in cracks in old walls or near drains. They are a fern, so they make spores.
items.why: A strong answer names a real plant, a real place and the right group, with a reason.

worksheets.title: Why Plants Live Where They Live (stretch)

items.p: Why can a deodar grow 50 metres tall, while most mosses stay a few centimetres tall?
opts: A deodar has veins with stiff walls that carry water up and hold the tree up
Mosses grow only in the dark
items.why: Veins with lignin carry water high and hold a tall body up. Mosses have no such veins, so water moves only over their surface, which works for a few centimetres.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 5 in Madurai, finds a small fern growing on a wall across the street from any other fern. Explain how the fern could have got there.
items.a: A fern somewhere nearby released spores into the air. The wind carried one spore to the damp wall. The spore grew into a tiny heart-shaped plant, and then into a new fern.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that spores are light enough for the wind to carry far, as the haldi was in the Fan Test.

items.p: A chilgoza pine nut grows inside a fruit, like a cashew.
items.why: False. A chilgoza is a naked seed. The chilgoza grows on the scale of a pine cone, with no fruit around it.

items.p: The seeds of a conifer sit on the scales of a ____, not inside a fruit.
items.why: Conifers make naked seeds on cone scales. Flowering plants make seeds inside fruits.

items.p: Sort these plants: which need a film of water for their male cells to swim to an egg, and which use pollen?
items.a: see items
items.why: Mosses and ferns need water, because their male cells swim. Pines, cycads, mangoes and rice use pollen, carried by wind or animals.

items.p: Shalini, a girl in Class 5, measured where her mustard seeds landed in the Fan Test: they landed 15 cm, 20 cm and 25 cm away. What is the average?
items.why: Add the three: 15 + 20 + 25 = 60. Divide by 3: 60 ÷ 3 = 20 cm. Choosing 60 means adding but forgetting to divide.

items.p: Use this table of features to draw a family tree of a moss, a fern, a pine and a mango. Moss: no veins, no seeds. Fern: veins, no seeds. Pine: veins, seeds, no flowers. Mango: veins, seeds, flowers.
items.a: A trunk that splits first with the moss on one branch. Then the fern splits off. Then the pine. The mango is on the last branch.
items.why: Each split happens where a new feature appears. A strong tree marks the split with the feature: veins, then seeds, then flowers.

items.p: A school textbook says seaweeds are plants. A botanist says they are not.
items.a: A strong answer separates 'makes food from sunlight', which many groups of living beings do, from 'is a close relative', which is what the family tree shows. It uses a fact from the unit: land plants came from green algae, but red and brown seaweeds sit on very different branches. It gives one fair point from the other side.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about where to draw a line. Green seaweeds are close relatives of land plants, and red and brown seaweeds are not, so the word depends on how you cut the tree.

views.says: Seaweeds are plants. They are green or brown and make food from sunlight, just like a tulsi.
Only land plants, which all came from one green alga, should be called plants. Red and brown seaweeds are on very different branches of the tree of life.

items.ask: Which do you agree with? Use a fact from the unit. Then give one fair point from the other side.

items.p: Put the life of a fern in order, starting from a spore.
a: A spore lands on damp soil
The spore grows into a tiny flat heart-shaped plant
A male cell swims through water to an egg on the heart
A young fern grows up from the heart
The grown fern makes brown dots full of new spores
items.why: A fern's life has two stages: a tiny heart-shaped plant, and the big fern we know.
items: A young fern grows up from the heart
A spore lands on damp soil
The grown fern makes brown dots full of new spores
A male cell swims through water to an egg on the heart
The spore grows into a tiny flat heart-shaped plant

items.p: Remember the Pine Cone Weather Test. A pine cone closes in wet weather and opens in dry weather. Explain how this helps the pine tree.
items.a: Pine seeds have papery wings. In dry air they fly far on the wind. In wet weather they would be heavy and fall close, so the cone keeps them in until it is dry.
items.why: A strong answer links the opening to the seeds' wings and to the weather.

items.p: Match each plant to a place in India where they grow.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These show that non-flowering plants grow all over India, not only in the hills.
pairs: the wet forests of the Western Ghats
eaten as a vegetable in Assam

items.p: A banyan tree is a flowering plant, but you never see their flowers. Where are they?
items.why: Banyans and peepals keep hundreds of tiny flowers inside each young fig. Tiny fig wasps crawl in and carry pollen.

items.p: Three of these have no veins. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The wall moss, the sphagnum moss and Marchantia (a liverwort) have no veins. The fern has veins, which is why ferns can grow much taller.

items.p: Label a drawing of a pine branch: needle leaves, small male cone that makes pollen, big female cone, and winged seed.
items.why: Pines have two kinds of cone. Small male cones make pollen. Bigger female cones hold the seeds on their scales.
items.art: A pine branch with two kinds of cones and a seed, with blank label lines.

items.p: In the Fan Test, the rajma barely moved. Give two ways that a big, heavy seed can still travel far from their parent.
items.a: A coconut floats on the sea. A mango seed is carried by an animal or a person who eats the fruit. A seed can also have hooks that stick to fur.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different real ways, such as water and animals, and an example of each.

items.p: Design an experiment to find out whether damp spores travel as far as dry ones. Use haldi as your spores. Say what you change, what you keep the same and what you measure.
items.a: Change: dry haldi, and haldi sprinkled with a few drops of water. Keep the same: height, drop spot, fan speed and amount. Measure: the farthest yellow on the paper track, 3 times each.
items.why: A strong design changes only one thing, keeps everything else the same, repeats each try and says what result would answer the question.

items.p: Scientists disagree about when flowering plants began. Charles Darwin called their sudden rise in the fossils 'an abominable mystery'.
items.a: A strong answer explains each side's evidence: fossils about 130 million years old, and DNA estimates that go much further back. It may suggest how both could be partly right, such as flowering plants starting early but staying rare.
items.why: This is still argued about. Both kinds of evidence are real, and each has limits.

views.says: The oldest flower fossils are about 130 million years old. So flowering plants began about then, and spread fast.
By measuring how fast DNA changes, we think flowering plants began much earlier, but stayed small and rare at first.

items.ask: Which scientist do you find more convincing? Why? What evidence could settle the question?

items.p: Orchid seeds are as fine as dust and carry almost no food. What do they need before they can sprout?
opts: A fungus that gives them food
A bird to eat them first
items.why: Orchid seeds are like spores: light enough to travel far, but with no food store. In nature, they sprout only with help from a fungus that feeds them.

items.p: Before seed plants, only mosses, ferns and their relatives lived on land. Explain why seed plants could spread into dry lands where they could not.
items.a: Seed plants use pollen, which travels by wind or animals, so their male cells don't need water to swim. Their seeds carry food and a tough coat, so they can wait in dry ground until rain comes.
items.why: A strong answer gives both reasons: pollen means the male cells need no water to travel, and seeds can survive dry times.

items.p: Cycads and the ginkgo tree still make male cells that swim, inside the pollen.
items.why: True. In 1896 two Japanese scientists, Sakugoro Hirase and Seiichiro Ikeno, found swimming male cells in the ginkgo and in cycads, one in each. Even so, they swim only a very short way, within the seed plant.

items.p: Glossopteris fossils are found in India, Africa, South America, Antarctica and Australia. Their seeds were too heavy to cross oceans. What does this show?
opts: The seeds were carried by ships
Each land had its own Glossopteris by chance
items.why: A plant with heavy seeds could only spread across one connected land. This was one of the clues that the continents have moved.

items.p: Long ago, ferns, mosses, algae and fungi were put into one group because none of them has flowers. Why is 'has no flowers' a poor way to make a group?
items.a: No flowers only says what the plants lack. Mosses and ferns turned out to be relatives of conifers, but fungi and algae are far away on the tree of life. A good group needs a shared ancestor, not a shared missing part.
items.why: A strong answer says that a group made from something missing can mix unrelated living beings, and that a shared ancestor is what makes a real group.

items.p: Much of India's coal formed from ancient ____ that were buried and squashed for millions of years.
items.why: Coal is the remains of plants that lived long ago, such as forests of Glossopteris, a seed plant without flowers. Buried deep and squashed for millions of years, they slowly turned into coal.

items.p: Sort each statement: is it true of spores, of seeds, or of both?
items.a: see items
items.why: A spore is one cell with almost no food. A seed is many cells with a young plant, a food store and a coat. Both can grow into a new plant and both can be carried away from the parent.
items: has a tough coat made of many cells
can grow into a new plant
is light enough for gentle wind to carry far
can be carried away from the parent

items.p: Botanists have named about 295,000 flowering plants, 12,000 mosses, 10,500 ferns and 1,000 conifers and their relatives. About what fraction of these plants are flowering plants?
items.why: The total is about 318,500. 295,000 is a little over 9 tenths of that. So about 9 in every 10 named plants flower.

items.p: Put these events in order, from the oldest to the most recent.
a: The first land plants, making spores (about 470 million years ago)
The first plants with veins (about 430 million years ago)
The first seeds (about 365 million years ago)
The first flowers (about 130 million years ago)
items.why: Each new feature appeared inside an older group: land plants, then veins, then seeds, then flowers. Humans came very late.
items: The first seeds (about 365 million years ago)
The first land plants, making spores (about 470 million years ago)
The first flowers (about 130 million years ago)
The first plants with veins (about 430 million years ago)

items.p: When a fern's spore cases dry out, they snap open and fling the spores out, fast. Some people say the fern senses dry air and chooses that moment. Others say it is only a mechanism, like a spring. Write both views, then say what you think.
items.a: Ferns sense the weather and release their spores when the air is dry, which is when spores fly best. Many scientists describe this as a mechanism: the walls of the spore case dry and bend until they snap. My view, with a reason.
items.why: A strong answer states both views fairly, and gives a reason for its own view. Both views agree on what happens. They differ on how to describe it.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are real scientists. Wilhelm Hofmeister never went to university, yet he changed how plants are understood.
pairs: showed that mosses, ferns and conifers follow one pattern of life
found swimming male cells in the ginkgo tree
studied fossil seed plants from the Rajmahal Hills in Jharkhand
studied mosses and helped start the New York Botanical Garden
explained how the veins inside plants are built

items.p: Which of these is not a seed?
items.why: A chilgoza, a mustard seed and a coconut are all seeds, with a young plant and food inside. A fern spore is a single cell.

items.p: Label a drawing of a fern's life: spore, heart-shaped little plant, young fern growing from the heart, grown fern with spore dots.
items.why: A strong label shows the circle of life: spore, heart, young fern, grown fern, and back to spores.
items.art: A circle of four drawings with blank label lines.

quiz.p: A friend says, 'Plants with no flowers cannot make seeds.' Which plant shows this is wrong?
opts: A deodar, which makes seeds on cones
quiz.why: Conifers like the deodar make seeds without flowers, on the scales of cones. Ferns and mosses make no seeds, so they don't prove the friend wrong.

quiz.p: What is inside a seed that is not inside a spore?
opts: A tiny young plant and a store of food
quiz.why: A seed is many cells: a young plant, food and a coat. A spore is one cell with almost no food. That is why seeds are heavier.

quiz.p: Fine haldi powder blown by a fan travels far. Heavy rajma drops close. Fern spores are as tiny and light as haldi grains. What does this tell us about fern spores?
opts: Being tiny and light, spores can be carried far by gentle wind
Spores never leave the parent fern
quiz.why: Haldi is about as fine as fern spores. Like the haldi, spores fall slowly, so even gentle wind carries them far.

quiz.p: You are using a key. The first question is 'Does the plant have flowers?' The answer is no. The next is 'Does the plant make cones?' The answer is no. The plant has fronds with veins. What is it?
quiz.why: No flowers, no cones, but veins and fronds: that is a fern. A moss would have no veins.

quiz.p: Why do most mosses grow only a few centimetres tall?
opts: They have no veins with stiff walls to carry water up and hold them up
quiz.why: Without veins, water moves only over the moss's surface, which works over a few centimetres. Ferns and trees have veins, so they can grow tall.

quiz.p: Why do mosses and ferns need water to make new plants, but pines do not?
opts: Moss and fern male cells must swim to an egg, but pine pollen is carried by wind
Mosses and ferns are thirsty all the time
quiz.why: In mosses and ferns, a male cell swims through a film of water to reach an egg. Seed plants use pollen, which needs no water to travel.

quiz.p: On a family tree of plants, why are a pine and a mango on the same branch?
opts: Both make seeds, which came from one shared ancestor
quiz.why: Seeds appeared once, and all seed plants came from that ancestor. Height and leaf shape do not show relatives.

quiz.p: Since the 1990s, what else have botanists used, besides body features, to group plants?
quiz.why: DNA carries the instructions passed from parent to young, so comparing DNA shows who is related to whom. It mostly agrees with groups made from features like seeds and veins.

quiz.p: Why do most botanists today avoid calling mosses 'lower plants'?
opts: Today's mosses have been changing for as long as flowering plants, and are very good at their own way of life
quiz.why: Mosses' ancestors came earlier, but living mosses are not unfinished plants. 'Lower' suggests a ladder, and a family tree is a bush.

quiz.p: Rekha, a girl in Class 5, wants to know if til travels farther than mustard in the Fan Test. Which test is fair?
opts: Drop both from the same height, at the same spot, with the same fan speed, 3 times each
Drop til from higher up because it is lighter
Use a fast fan for til and a slow one for mustard
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes: what is dropped. Repeating 3 times guards against a fluke.

applications: Farmers in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and many other states grow Azolla, a tiny water fern, as cattle feed and to add nitrogen to rice fields. A microbe living inside Azolla takes nitrogen from the air.
Gardeners pack sphagnum moss around orchid roots and line hanging baskets with moss, because moss holds water for a long time.
Pine timber is used for furniture and boxes, and resin from chir pine in Uttarakhand and Himachal is made into turpentine.
Much of India's coal formed from ancient forests of seed plants without flowers, such as Glossopteris.
The ladder fern Pteris vittata soaks up arsenic from soil. Scientists are testing such ferns to clean soils polluted with arsenic, a problem in parts of West Bengal and Bihar.
Botanists use keys, and now DNA tests, to identify plants, for example to check which plants are really in a packet of herbal medicine.
Seed banks store dry seeds for many years, which works because a seed can wait alive until water comes. Spores of many ferns can be stored too.

open_questions.q: Why did flowering plants spread so fast, about 130 million years ago?
open_questions.why_open: Fossils and DNA give different dates for when they began, and nobody knows for sure what made them take over so quickly.

open_questions.q: What did the very first land plant look like?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest land plant fossils are only spores. The plants that made them have not been found.

open_questions.q: Did the first land plants need fungi to survive on land?
open_questions.why_open: Some of the oldest plant fossils, about 407 million years old, already have fungi living inside them. Whether plants could have come onto land without fungi is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of plants are there?
open_questions.why_open: About 2,000 new plant species are named every year, and many places, such as the forests of Northeast India, are still not fully explored.

open_questions.q: How does a dried-out moss revive within hours of rain?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the chemicals involved, but not the whole story of how the cells protect themselves and switch back on.

maths.problem: In the Fan Test, the haldi travelled 180 cm, 210 cm and 240 cm in three tries. What is the average distance?
maths.explain: Add the three tries: 180 + 210 + 240 = 630. Divide by the number of tries: 630 ÷ 3 = 210. So the average is 210 cm.
maths.context: This is about the Fan Test, where you drop haldi and seeds in front of a fan and measure how far they travel.

chart.title: Made-up example: haldi distance in three tries

maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. An average of three tries gives a number we can trust more.

maths.problem: In the Fan Test, the haldi travelled 210 cm on average and the mustard 20 cm. About how many times as far did the haldi travel?
maths.explain: 210 ÷ 20 = 10.5. So the haldi travelled about 10 times as far as the mustard.
maths.context: This is about the Fan Test, where you drop haldi and seeds in front of a fan and measure how far they travel.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'about 10 times as far' compares the two results more clearly than just saying 'farther'.

maths.problem: Botanists have named about 295,000 flowering plants, 12,000 mosses, 10,500 ferns and 1,000 conifers and their relatives. What percentage of these are flowering plants?
maths.explain: Total: 295,000 + 12,000 + 10,500 + 1,000 = 318,500. Flowering plants: 295,000 ÷ 318,500 is about 0.93. So about 93 out of every 100 are flowering plants.
maths.context: This is about how many kinds of plant are in each big group.

chart.title: Named plant species in each group (rounded)

maths.why_maths: A percentage shows at once how much bigger one group is than all the others put together.

maths.problem: You make a timeline strip of plants on land, 47 cm long, from 470 million years ago to today. How far from the 'today' end do you mark the first seeds, 365 million years ago, and the first flowers, 130 million years ago?
maths.answer: Seeds at 36.5 cm, flowers at 13 cm from the 'today' end.
maths.explain: 47 cm stands for 470 million years, so 1 cm stands for 10 million years. 365 ÷ 10 = 36.5 cm. 130 ÷ 10 = 13 cm.
maths.context: This is about the order in which the big plant groups appeared.
maths.why_maths: Huge spans of time are impossible to picture. A scale shrinks them onto a strip you can see, so you notice that flowers are a recent arrival.

maths.problem: On a pine cone, Bornali, a girl in Class 5, counted 8 spirals going one way and 13 going the other. In the pattern 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, each number is the sum of the two before it. What are the next two numbers?
maths.explain: 8 + 13 = 21. 13 + 21 = 34. Sunflower heads often have 21 and 34, or 34 and 55, spirals.
maths.context: This is about the Pine Cone Weather Test, where you also count the spirals of scales on a cone.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you predict spirals on other cones and seed heads before you count them.

maths.problem: In the Moss Sponge test, 200 ml of water went in with the moss. 110 ml was left after the moss was lifted out. With the soil, 180 ml was left. How much more water did the moss hold than the soil?
maths.explain: The moss held 200 − 110 = 90 ml. The soil held 200 − 180 = 20 ml. 90 − 20 = 70 ml more.
maths.context: This is about the Moss Sponge test, where you compare how much water moss and dry soil hold.
maths.why_maths: We can't measure the water inside the moss directly, so we measure what was left and work back.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out where ferns and mosses come from? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1753 the Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus sorted plants by counting the parts of their flowers. Ferns, mosses, algae and fungi had no flowers to count, so he put them all into one group. He called it Cryptogamia, 'hidden marriage', because nobody knew how they made new plants. In Europe, many people still believed ferns had invisible seeds. In the 1840s, botanists watched fern spores grow into tiny heart-shaped plants. Then a young man in Leipzig, Wilhelm Hofmeister, studied mosses, ferns and conifers under his microscope. He had never been to university. He worked in his father's music shop and studied plants in his spare time. In 1851 he published a book showing that mosses, ferns and conifers all follow one pattern. Each life has a spore-making stage and an egg-and-sperm stage. In conifers the second stage is hidden inside the cone and the pollen. So the 'hidden' plants were not a separate world. They were relatives of the seed plants, with the same plan of life. The University of Rostock gave him an honorary doctorate, and in 1863 he became a professor.
how_we_found_out.who: Carl Linnaeus, a Swedish botanist; Wilhelm Hofmeister, a German botanist who taught himself
how_we_found_out.when: 1753 (Linnaeus), the 1840s (fern spores watched as they grew) and 1851 (Hofmeister)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That ferns and mosses were a separate, mysterious kind of plant with hidden or invisible seeds. Hofmeister showed that they follow the same pattern of life as conifers, only without seeds.
how_we_found_out.art: A young man at a wooden desk beside sheet music and a brass microscope, with drawings of a moss, a fern and a pine cone on his page.
